newsitem.title: FRANCE: Cracks appear in French anti-privatisation stand.
newsitem.headline: Cracks appear in French anti-privatisation stand.

text.p: After talking tough during the election campaign, France's new Socialist government is finding it hard to live up to its anti-privatisation stand in the face of economic constraints.

Cracks have already appeared with Finance Minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn telling Socialist parliamentarians he was "not against" opening up the capital of telecoms giant France Telecom as long as staff were consulted over the move.

Prime Minister Lionel Jospin has also shown signs of back-pedalling. He told parliament last week he did not support the sale of big government-owned companies operating in the competitive sector -- among which he numbered telecoms, electronics and "other sectors".

But he left himself an escape hatch, saying he knew "adaptations will be needed to maintain our place among the world's most highly developed nations" and that he would look to "the national interest".
The comments were interpreted by financial analysts as a sign that while full privatisations might not be in the cards, partial sales could be.
The reasons for the Socialists softening their stand are not hard to fathom -- even though it could cause a rift with their Communists allies on whom they depend for their parliamentary majority.
The government has promised to take France into European monetary union without fresh austerity but now must balance the books.

The government will need the money generated by the sale of minority stake in France Telecom to boost the balance sheets of ailing state-owned companies, such as insurer GAN, which is in line for a 20 billion franc handout.
Daily Liberation reported on Thursday that the official line is that there will be no privatisation of defence electronics firm Thomson-CSF and troubled flag carrier Air France.

But it said there are voices in government circles suggesting that the state could cut its holding to a minority stake and keep a "golden share" which would allow it to block decisions it did not like and protect state interests.
Analysts have taken heart from Jospin's comments in favour of consolidation in the defence sector last week and of the need to adopt a new, more coherent policy for the industry.
Jospin's comments were echoed by Industry Minister Christian Pierret who said on Thursday that France's big industrial sectors were too dispersed to function well internationally.
"In aeronautics or electronics we need to regroup, especially on the European level," he told Liberation, leaving open the question of ownership.

If Jospin decides to go ahead with some privatisations, he has allies. Socialist former European Commission president Jacques Delors said last weekend he favored "opening up the capital" of France Telecom so "this magnificent group...can forge all types of alliances."
Delors also said Air France staff can only be "made to understand the nature of competition today if the company is privatised".
Former Communist transport minister Charles Fiterman, now an independent leftist, has also swung his weight behind opening up the capital of public companies.

"What matters is not the ownership structure but a strategy in the service of the company and the country," he said this weekend. "We have to get out of the religious debate over nationalisation versus privatisation."
